q.t: What are European laws called?
q.e: The UK joined the European Economic Community in 1973. European laws are called directives, regulations or framework decisions.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Membership of the Commonwealth is voluntary, and the Commonwealth can suspend a member.
q.e: Membership is voluntary. The Commonwealth has no power over its members, although it can suspend membership. The Commonwealth is based on the core values of democracy, good government and the rule of law.

q.t: Which TWO are core values of the Commonwealth, according to the handbook?
q.e: The Commonwealth has no power over its members, although it can suspend membership. The Commonwealth is based on the core values of democracy, good government and the rule of law.

q.t: On what date was the Treaty of Rome signed, and what did it create?
q.e: The European Union, originally called the European Economic Community (EEC), was set up by six western European countries who signed the Treaty of Rome on 25 March 1957.
o: 25 March 1957, creating the European Economic Community
25 March 1973, creating the European Economic Community
25 March 1957, creating the Council of Europe

q.t: Which TWO countries were among the six founder members of the EEC?
q.e: The European Union, originally called the European Economic Community, was set up by six western European countries: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

q.t: In which year did the UK become a member of the European Economic Community?
q.e: West Germany, France, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands formed the European Economic Community (EEC) in 1957. At first the UK did not wish to join the EEC but it eventually did so in 1973.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: The Council of Europe is separate from the EU. It has 47 member countries, including the UK, and is responsible for the protection and promotion of human rights in those countries. It has no power to make laws but draws up conventions and charters.
o: The Council of Europe has no power to make laws
The Council of Europe makes laws that bind its member countries

q.t: How many member countries does the Council of Europe have?
q.e: The Council of Europe is separate from the EU. It has 47 member countries, including the UK, and is responsible for the protection and promotion of human rights in those countries.

q.t: Which convention is the best known drawn up by the Council of Europe?
q.e: It has no power to make laws but draws up conventions and charters, the most well-known of which is the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, usually called the European Convention on Human Rights.
o: The European Convention on Human Rights

q.t: When was the United Nations set up, and what does it aim to do?
q.e: The UK is part of the United Nations (UN), an international organisation with more than 190 countries as members. The UN was set up after the Second World War and aims to prevent war and promote international peace and security.
o: After the Second World War, to prevent war and promote international peace and security
After the First World War, to prevent war and promote international peace
In 1957, to promote trade between European countries
In 1973, to protect human rights in Europe

q.t: How many members are there on the UN Security Council, and what is the UK's position?
q.e: There are 15 members on the UN Security Council, which recommends action when there are international crises and threats to peace. The UK is one of five permanent members of the Security Council.
o: 15 members, and the UK is one of five permanent members
five members, and the UK is one of 15 permanent members
15 members, and the UK is one of ten permanent members
27 members, and the UK is one of five permanent members

q.t: What have NATO members agreed to do?
q.e: The UK is also a member of NATO. NATO is a group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if they come under attack. It also aims to maintain peace between all of its members.
o: To help each other if they come under attack
To draw up conventions on human rights
To abolish taxes on imported goods

q.t: In which year did the UK sign the European Convention on Human Rights?
q.e: British diplomats and lawyers had an important role in drafting the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The UK was one of the first countries to sign the Convention in 1950.

q.t: Which Act incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law?
q.e: The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. The government, public bodies and the courts must follow the principles of the Convention.

q.t: In which THREE documents do British rights have their roots, according to the handbook?
q.e: Britain has a long history of respecting an individual's rights and ensuring essential freedoms. These rights have their roots in Magna Carta, the Habeas Corpus Act and the Bill of Rights of 1689.
o: Magna Carta, the Habeas Corpus Act and the Bill of Rights
The Treaty of Rome, the Beveridge Report and the Human Rights Act
The Domesday Book, Magna Carta and the Act of Union
The Statute of Rhuddlan, the Bill of Rights and the Reform Act

q.t: Which TWO of these are principles included in the European Convention on Human Rights?
q.e: Some of the principles included in the European Convention on Human Rights are: right to life, prohibition of torture, prohibition of slavery and forced labour, right to liberty and security, right to a fair trial, freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and freedom of expression.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Arranged marriages, where both parties agree to the marriage, are acceptable in the UK.
q.e: A marriage should be entered into with the full and free consent of both people involved. Arranged marriages, where both parties agree to the marriage, are acceptable in the UK. Forced marriage is where one or both parties do not or cannot give their consent, and forcing another person to marry is a criminal offence.

q.t: Anyone found to have breached a Forced Marriage Protection Order can be jailed for how long?
q.e: A potential victim, or someone acting for them, can apply for an order. Anyone found to have breached an order can be jailed for up to two years for contempt of court.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Female genital mutilation (FGM), also known as cutting or female circumcision, is illegal in the UK. Practising FGM or taking a girl or woman abroad for FGM is a criminal offence.
o: Taking a girl or woman abroad for FGM is a criminal offence
FGM is only an offence if it is carried out inside the UK

q.t: Which TWO of these does money raised from income tax pay for, according to the handbook?
q.e: Money raised from income tax pays for government services such as roads, education, police and the armed forces. National Insurance Contributions pay for state benefits and services such as the state retirement pension and the NHS.

q.t: What is the system called by which most employees have income tax taken from their pay?
q.e: For most people, the right amount of income tax is automatically taken from their income from employment by their employer and paid directly to HM Revenue & Customs. This system is called 'Pay As You Earn' (PAYE). If you are self-employed, you need to pay your own tax through a system called 'self-assessment'.

q.t: When are young people in the UK sent a National Insurance number?
q.e: A National Insurance number is a unique personal account number. It makes sure that the National Insurance Contributions and tax you pay are properly recorded against your name. All young people in the UK are sent a National Insurance number just before their 16th birthday.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
A National Insurance number on its own proves to an employer that you have the right to work in the UK.
q.e: A non-UK national living in the UK and looking for work will need a National Insurance number. However, you can start work without one. A National Insurance number does not on its own prove to an employer that you have the right to work in the UK.

q.t: Which TWO of these are freedoms the UK offers, according to the handbook?
q.e: In return, the UK offers freedom of belief and religion, freedom of speech, freedom from unfair discrimination, a right to a fair trial, and a right to join in the election of a government.
o: Freedom to ignore laws you disagree with
